items.prompt: A problem asks for an optimal sequence of irrevocable decisions. Which statements are genuine structural reasons to investigate a greedy strategy? Select all statements that apply.
constraints: A decision cannot be undone after it is committed.
The objective is global, not merely the value of the next action.

options.text: The input records can be sorted by at least one field.
A locally preferred feasible choice may be replaceable for the corresponding choice in some optimal solution without worsening the objective.
It is possible to imagine an implementation with one loop.
After fixing that choice, the remaining work has the same optimization contract under an updated boundary or state.

feedback.reason: A credible greedy candidate needs a potentially safe local commitment and a residual problem that can be solved under the same objective. Sortability and loop count are implementation facts, not correctness structure.

blocks.text:
Greedy reasoning is about committing now without later reconsideration. The first accepted statement identifies the greedy-choice property: the preferred choice must be compatible with at least one global optimum, commonly shown by exchange, dominance, or a stays-ahead argument. The second identifies the recursive structure needed after that commitment: once the choice is fixed, the rest of the instance must still express the same objective with a smaller feasible region.

Neither condition is established by syntax. Almost any finite record set can be sorted, and many incorrect heuristics can be written as one pass. When transferring this test, ask two questions before naming a strategy: “Why can this choice be fixed without losing an optimum?” and “What exactly is the remaining instance after the choice?” If either answer is missing, greedy is only a hypothesis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sortable_input: Sorting may expose a useful order, but every proposed sort key still needs a correctness argument. Sortability alone says nothing about whether the first sorted item is safe to commit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_pass_possible: A one-pass procedure may still make irreversible mistakes. Loop count describes an implementation shape, not the dominance or exchange property required for greedy correctness.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.exchange_safe_candidate: Without a reason that an optimum can include the local choice, the method may discard every optimal solution at its first commitment.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.same_form_residual: Without a well-defined residual problem, later choices may depend on hidden history and require state-based optimization rather than repeated greedy selection.

items.prompt: You must choose as many mutually non-overlapping half-open intervals [start, end) as possible. Which observation most strongly supports treating the problem as a greedy candidate?
constraints: Every selected interval contributes exactly one unit to the objective.
Touching endpoints are compatible: an interval starting at the current end is allowed.

options.text: The shortest feasible interval consumes the least duration, so it must belong to an optimum.
Because intervals overlap, dynamic programming and greedy are interchangeable descriptions of the same method.
An earliest-finishing feasible interval can replace the first interval of an optimal schedule while leaving no less room for all later intervals.
The earliest-starting interval begins first, so delaying that choice cannot help.

feedback.reason: The replaceability of the earliest-finishing interval is the decisive signal. It connects the local choice to an optimum and defines the remaining instance by a single end boundary.

blocks.text:
The objective counts intervals, not occupied time. Let an optimal schedule begin with interval o and let g be a feasible interval with the earliest end. Because g.end is no later than o.end, every interval that can follow o can also follow g under the half-open endpoint contract. Replacing o with g therefore preserves both feasibility and the number of selected intervals. The remaining task is the same problem restricted to intervals whose start is at least g.end.

This is stronger than noticing that the input contains intervals. Shortest duration and earliest start do not control the future boundary that determines later feasibility. The recognition transfers to equivalent maximum-cardinality or minimum-removal formulations with equal item value. It stops transferring when intervals have different weights, because a one-for-one replacement can preserve count while reducing total value.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shortest_duration_local: Short duration is plausible because it sounds economical, but a short interval may finish late and block two compatible intervals. Duration is not the decisive future boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.earliest_start_local: Starting early does not imply finishing early. An early-starting long interval can occupy the resource while several later intervals could have been selected.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.overlap_requires_dp: Overlap creates a feasibility relation, but it does not make methods interchangeable. Greedy is justified here by exchange; weighted or state-dependent variants may instead require dynamic programming.

items.prompt: A route has one decision at each station. The immediate fee of a coupon is known, but the discount available at the next station depends on the last two coupon types chosen. The goal is minimum total fee. What is the best strategy-level conclusion?
constraints: Coupon choices are irrevocable.
Two partial routes at the same station can have different future discounts because their last two coupon types differ.

options.text: Choose the cheapest coupon at every station; a smaller immediate fee always improves the final total.
Sort coupon types by fee once and always take the first currently available type.
The problem is not yet a justified greedy candidate because the cheapest current coupon may change future costs through history-dependent state.
Use either greedy or dynamic programming; both optimize the same objective and are therefore interchangeable.

feedback.reason: The future value of a coupon is not determined by its immediate fee alone. Different histories remain materially distinct, so an irrevocable local minimum needs a new dominance proof before it can be called greedy-safe.

blocks.text:
A greedy boundary should summarize everything about the past that matters for future feasibility and objective value. Here the current station index is not enough: the last two coupon types alter the transition costs that remain. Choosing the smallest immediate fee can move the route into a more expensive future state, while a slightly larger fee can unlock better discounts later.

This does not prove that no specialized greedy theorem exists, but it removes the ordinary signal for a repeated local minimum. The natural diagnostic is to retain the relevant history as state and compare alternative continuations. That is the role a dynamic-programming formulation might serve; designing that state is outside this item. The transfer rule is to look for multiple partial solutions that reach the same visible position but have different future option values. Their coexistence is a warning that “current cheapest” is not a sufficient decision rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pick_cheapest_coupon: Immediate fee is only part of the consequence. This option ignores that the selected coupon changes the prices of later choices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_coupon_types: A fixed ordering cannot account for history-dependent availability and transition costs. Sorting is useful only when the sort key remains decisive throughout the residual problem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.greedy_equals_dp: The methods have different commitments. Dynamic programming may retain several states; greedy discards alternatives and therefore needs a proof that the discarded histories cannot win.

items.prompt: Each job has a duration and a deadline, all jobs are available initially, and the objective is to complete the largest possible number by their deadlines. A candidate method processes jobs by deadline, tentatively keeps each job, and removes one selected job whenever the prefix becomes infeasible. Which observation identifies the greedy structure?
constraints: Every completed job contributes the same value of one.
A job counts only if its completion time is no later than its deadline.

options.text: Using a heap makes the method greedy and therefore proves that it is optimal.
The earliest-deadline job must be permanently kept because it appears first after sorting.
Within an infeasible deadline prefix, removing the longest selected duration creates the greatest time reduction while decreasing the selected count by exactly one.
Selecting all jobs globally by shortest duration is equivalent to processing deadline prefixes.

feedback.reason: The signal is a reversible local repair on a deadline-ordered prefix: discard the longest selected job to preserve the best time budget for the same retained count. The heap only implements that choice.

blocks.text:
Deadline order exposes the constraints incrementally. After considering a prefix, the candidate solution represents jobs that could fit within the deadlines seen so far. If adding a job makes the total duration too large, one job must be removed to restore a feasible cardinality. Removing the longest selected duration minimizes the total time of the remaining set among all one-job removals, so it leaves the strongest feasible prefix for future deadlines.

This is a greedy-with-heap pattern because the set of candidates changes as deadlines are reached and the decisive extreme must be queried repeatedly. The heap is not the proof; it is an efficient data structure for the proven local repair. The recognition stops transferring when jobs have unequal rewards, dependencies, or constraints that are not captured by each deadline prefix, because removing one longest job may then discard disproportionate value or fail to repair the relevant constraint.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.heap_implies_correctness: A heap efficiently returns an extreme element, but it does not establish that the extreme is safe to discard. Correctness comes from the prefix invariant and equal-cardinality objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_earliest_deadline_only: Deadline order determines when a constraint becomes active, not which job is immune from removal. A long early-deadline job may be the best job to discard from an infeasible prefix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.choose_shortest_globally: Global shortest-duration order ignores which deadlines are currently binding. The prefix method combines deadline exposure with a separate removal criterion.

items.prompt: Two tasks both say “select as many objects as possible.” Task A selects non-overlapping unweighted intervals. Task B selects projects, but every pair of selected projects can add a compatibility bonus or penalty. Which comparison is correct?
constraints: Task A uses half-open intervals and equal value per selected interval.
Task B has arbitrary pairwise interactions not reducible to a single ordering boundary.

options.text: Both tasks maximize a count, so the same local rule must solve both.
Task A has a credible exchange boundary; Task B is not a greedy candidate merely because the surface objective uses the same words.
Pairwise bonuses make Task B more suitable for greedy selection because each choice has more local information.
Sort both inputs by one numeric field; the first item after sorting is the greedy choice in each task.

feedback.reason: Greedy classification follows the interaction structure, not the wording of the objective. A single interval end can summarize future feasibility in Task A, while Task B retains set-dependent interactions.

blocks.text:
In unweighted interval selection, the consequences of the first choice can be summarized by one boundary: the end of the selected interval. An earliest-finishing choice can be exchanged into an optimum, and the residual instance remains another interval-selection problem. Task B has no comparable summary under the stated assumptions. Adding or removing one project changes several pairwise contributions, so the apparent value of a project depends on which other projects are selected.

The important transfer habit is to preserve the mechanism while varying the surface. Similar verbs such as “select,” “maximize,” or “schedule” do not imply the same strategy. Greedy recognition transfers only when the new context retains a safe local dominance relation and a residual state that captures all future consequences. Arbitrary pair interactions are a boundary signal that alternatives may need to remain visible to a state-based or combinatorial method.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_objective_same_strategy: An objective label does not determine the dependency structure. The same count objective can be easy under interval compatibility and hard under arbitrary interactions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.task_b_more_greedy: More local data is not the same as a safe local choice. Pairwise effects make the consequence of a choice depend on the rest of the set.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_decides_both: A sort key is useful only if it induces a dominance or exchange property. Task B provides no such field under the stated arbitrary interaction model.

items.prompt: A resource-allocation problem has a current feasible boundary b. After selecting candidate x, every future candidate that was feasible after a smaller boundary remains feasible after x. Which signal does this provide?
constraints: The objective contribution of each selected candidate is identical.
The residual problem depends on the boundary, not on hidden details of the discarded prefix.

options.text: The monotone boundary is a greedy signal: a choice that leaves the earliest or smallest feasible boundary can dominate later choices under the equal-value objective.
Every feasible boundary is equally good because the future can always be ignored.
The existence of a boundary proves that sorting the input is sufficient without comparing candidates.
A monotone boundary rules out greedy because a boundary can only be explored by backtracking.

feedback.reason: A dominating residual boundary is the mechanism that can make an irreversible local choice safe.

blocks.text:
The key observation is not merely that a boundary exists, but that an earlier or smaller boundary leaves a superset of the future feasible region. With equal contribution per selected item, replacing a choice by one that leaves no less future room preserves the current count and cannot reduce the best possible suffix. That relation is a candidate exchange or dominance proof.

The author still needs to state which direction is better and prove that the candidate is feasible, but the signal is structurally meaningful. Sorting can expose the order but cannot replace the comparison argument. The transfer test is to ask whether one partial solution dominates another by the exact state that controls every future transition; if yes, discarding the dominated state may be safe.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_boundary_is_optimal: Different boundaries can leave different future option sets. The dominance relation, not feasibility alone, gives the greedy signal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_is_proof: Ordering is an implementation aid. The proof must connect the chosen order to the future feasible region and objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.boundary_requires_backtracking: A monotone boundary often enables a forward scan; backtracking is needed only when no safe discard rule has been proved.

items.prompt: A candidate strategy chooses one item at a time. Two partial solutions reach the same position and have the same current score, but one leaves a strictly larger set of future feasible choices. What should pattern recognition infer?
constraints: Future score depends only on which choices remain feasible from the position.
The two partial solutions have no other hidden state affecting transitions.

options.text: The solution with fewer future choices is dominated and can be discarded, which is a strong greedy or state-compression signal.
Both states must be retained because any difference in future options makes greedy impossible.
The states are interchangeable solely because their current scores match.
Keep the solution with fewer prior decisions regardless of its future feasible set.

feedback.reason: Equal current score plus a superset of future feasible choices gives a dominance relation that safely removes one alternative under the stated state contract.

blocks.text:
If both partial solutions have the same visible position and current score, but every continuation available to the smaller set is also available to the larger set, the larger-feasible-set solution can simulate every future continuation of the other. It therefore cannot finish worse. This is the kind of dominance that justifies state compression or an irrevocable greedy preference.

Matching current scores alone is insufficient when future options differ in the opposite direction. A shorter history has no intrinsic value unless the objective or transitions reward it. The transfer test is to compare partial solutions using both accumulated objective and the complete future-relevant state; only a proven componentwise dominance relation licenses discarding one.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.retain_both_always: Different future sets do not automatically require both states. Here one future set contains the other and current scores tie, so one state dominates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.current_score_only: The same current score can lead to different final scores when future choices differ. Future reachability is part of the comparison.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.choose_shorter_history: History length is not the objective and may have no relation to future value or feasibility.

items.prompt: A problem asks for a minimum-cost feasible set. A proposed rule always chooses the currently cheapest item, but adding an item can unlock a discount on a later item and the discount depends on the chosen item type. What is the correct recognition result?
constraints: The discount can outweigh the current price difference.
The future transition state is not summarized by the current total cost alone.

options.text: The local price is not a sufficient greedy key; history-dependent discounts are a warning that competing states may need to be compared.
The cheapest item is safe because all costs are nonnegative.
Sort item types by price and keep that order; future discounts cannot affect the first decision.
Ignore discounts during selection and apply them after the set is built.

feedback.reason: Nonnegative immediate costs do not make the cheapest choice safe when the choice changes future prices.

blocks.text:
A greedy key must control the total consequence of a commitment, not only its immediate contribution. Here the item type changes the future discount, so two prefixes with the same current cost can have different optimal continuations. The cheaper prefix can be globally worse if it loses a valuable discount. That is a structural warning against treating current price as a sufficient key.

This observation does not by itself prove that dynamic programming is the final method, but it does mean a new dominance or exchange theorem is required before greedy selection is justified. The transfer test is to inspect whether the local choice changes future transition rules. If it does, retain or compare the relevant state unless a proof shows that one state dominates all alternatives.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cheapest_always_safe: Nonnegative costs prevent negative-cost anomalies but do not prevent a cheap choice from losing a larger future discount.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_by_price_only: A static price order ignores the type-dependent transition state and therefore has no established safety property.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.discount_is_postprocessing: The discount affects which choices are optimal, so postponing it changes the selection problem rather than solving it.

items.prompt: A candidate algorithm repeatedly selects the feasible interval with the earliest end. Which additional fact is needed to recognize the classic maximum-cardinality greedy structure rather than merely a plausible heuristic?
constraints: Every selected interval contributes the same value.
The residual problem consists of intervals starting at or after the selected end.

options.text: For any optimal schedule, the first interval can be replaced by the feasible earliest-finishing interval without reducing the number of remaining selectable intervals.
The rule is recognized as correct because the word “earliest” sounds conservative.
Any sort by end time is sufficient; the order itself proves that the first item is safe.
The selected interval must also have the shortest duration among all intervals.

feedback.reason: The recognition signal is the exchange that preserves or enlarges the residual feasible set, not the superficial appearance of the sort key.

blocks.text:
Let g be the feasible interval with the earliest end and let o be the first interval of an optimum. Since g.end is no later than o.end, every interval that follows o also follows g. Replacing o with g preserves one selected interval and leaves a residual instance with at least as many possibilities. Repeating the argument establishes the greedy structure.

Sorting by end time makes the candidate easy to find, but sorting is not the proof. The interval need not have the shortest duration; a short interval that ends later can leave less room. The transfer test is to identify the exact future boundary controlled by the local key and then state the one-for-one replacement that preserves the objective.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.earliest_end_looks_small: Intuitive conservatism is not a universal argument. The safety comes from the residual-set containment proved by the exchange.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.intervals_are_sorted: A sorted order only supplies candidates in an order; it does not show that accepting the first is compatible with an optimum.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shortest_interval: Earliest finish and shortest duration are different keys. Duration does not necessarily determine the future boundary.

items.prompt: Two variants process the same intervals by earliest finish. Variant A maximizes the number of selected intervals. Variant B maximizes the sum of interval weights. What recognition warning is correct?
constraints: Intervals are otherwise subject to the same non-overlap rule.
Weights are arbitrary and are not determined by interval length or finish time.

options.text: The count-preserving earliest-finish exchange supports Variant A but does not automatically preserve total weight in Variant B.
The proof transfers unchanged because both variants use the same feasibility rule.
Arbitrary weights strengthen earliest finish because valuable intervals should always end sooner.
Ignore weights while selecting and add them afterward; the selected count determines the weighted optimum.

feedback.reason: The classic exchange preserves one selected interval, not an arbitrary weighted contribution.

blocks.text:
For maximum cardinality, replacing an optimum's first interval with an earlier-finishing one keeps the number selected and leaves at least as much room for the suffix. In the weighted variant, the replacement can remove a high-weight interval and therefore lower the objective even though it leaves more room. Feasibility preservation alone is not objective preservation.

The weighted problem may still admit another algorithm or additional assumptions, but the unweighted greedy proof cannot be reused automatically. The transfer test is to name the exact quantity preserved by the exchange. If the proof says “one interval for one interval” while the new objective sums arbitrary weights, the strategy classification must be reopened.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_proof_both: The feasibility part transfers, but the exchange no longer preserves the weighted objective. A new theorem is required.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.weights_make_end_more_decisive: Arbitrary weight is independent of finish time; an early finish can be low value while a later interval is highly valuable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.remove_all_weights: Weights are the objective in Variant B. Ignoring them can select a schedule with fewer total points despite good cardinality.

items.prompt: Which signal suggests a problem may have a greedy candidate rather than requiring arbitrary backtracking?
constraints: A local choice can be compared by a boundary or priority.
The choice appears to restrict future options.

options.text: A candidate appears to leave a frontier that dominates the alternatives while preserving the objective contribution.
options.explanation: This is the shape an exchange proof would formalize.

options.text: Any problem with a locally largest value is greedy by definition.
options.explanation: Immediate value need not dominate future combinations.

options.text: A small input automatically makes greedy correct.
options.explanation: Input size affects cost, not the theorem.

options.text: The presence of a sort operation proves the problem is greedy.
options.explanation: Sorting is used by many non-greedy algorithms.

feedback.reason: Greedy recognition is a hypothesis about future-state dominance.

blocks.text: Look for a local choice that leaves a no-worse feasible frontier and an exchange that preserves value. Without those signals, backtracking, dynamic programming, or other strategies may be needed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_local_best: Immediate value need not dominate future combinations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.small_input: Input size affects cost, not the theorem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_present: Sorting is used by many non-greedy algorithms.

items.prompt: Why is a compact boundary state an important greedy-recognition signal?
constraints: Future feasibility depends on a small summary of prior choices.
The local choice can improve or preserve that summary.

options.text: If two partial solutions have the same objective and one leaves a no-worse boundary, they can share the same future analysis.
options.explanation: This creates the dominance relation behind an exchange proof.

options.text: A compact state is irrelevant because greedy proofs must remember every prior choice.
options.explanation: Sufficient-state compression is often what makes greedy possible.

options.text: Any smaller numeric boundary is safe regardless of hidden constraints.
options.explanation: The boundary must be sufficient and tied to the proof.

options.text: The signal concerns only implementation memory, not correctness.
options.explanation: State sufficiency is a semantic property.

feedback.reason: Greedy choices often work because future decisions see an equivalent or dominated boundary state.

blocks.text: For interval scheduling, an earlier end leaves a superset of feasible suffixes. The same shape appears in other problems, but the state must be proven sufficient rather than assumed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_history: Sufficient-state compression is often what makes greedy possible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.boundary_value: The boundary must be sufficient and tied to the proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memory_only: State sufficiency is a semantic property.

items.prompt: What evidence is still missing after several examples support a greedy rule?
constraints: The goal is a universal optimality claim.
Examples cover only selected inputs.

options.text: Either prove an exchange or dominance property for arbitrary optimal solutions or find a legal counterexample; examples alone are not enough.
Generate more random examples until the success rate is high enough.
Benchmark the implementation because speed validates the strategy.
Sort the passing examples so the pattern becomes a proof.
options.explanation: Reordering examples does not quantify over all inputs.

feedback.reason: Recognition should lead directly to proof obligations, not to confidence from examples.

blocks.text: The next step is to identify what an arbitrary optimum can exchange with the proposed greedy choice and whether feasibility and objective are preserved. If that fails, the candidate is not established.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_examples: Reordering examples does not quantify over all inputs.

items.prompt: Which signal is evidence against a simple greedy solution?
constraints: A local choice can sacrifice multiple future combinations.
The objective rewards global combinations rather than one-step progress.

options.text: There is no apparent dominance relation and a local commitment can destroy incomparable future options; dynamic programming or search may be more appropriate.
options.explanation: Greedy needs a safe way to collapse those alternatives.

options.text: Sorting is possible, so greedy must be correct.
options.explanation: Sorting can be preprocessing for many approaches.

options.text: Positive values always make every optimization greedy.
options.explanation: Positivity supports some window proofs, not arbitrary greedy choices.

options.text: The algorithm makes one choice at a time, which proves it is greedy-correct.
options.explanation: Sequential choices can still be wrong without a proof.

feedback.reason: A simple greedy rule is suspect when local choices create incomparable future states.

blocks.text: The absence of dominance is a reason to preserve alternatives, often through a state representation. It does not prove that no greedy theorem exists, but it rejects an unsupported simple rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_available: Sorting can be preprocessing for many approaches.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.positive_values: Positivity supports some window proofs, not arbitrary greedy choices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_choice: Sequential choices can still be wrong without a proof.

items.prompt: Which objective shape is often compatible with a greedy candidate when local gains can be compared independently?

options.text: The objective is additive or admits a dominance comparison after each choice.
The objective depends on an unknown global interaction with no state summary.
The objective changes independently of every choice.
The objective is determined by variable names.

feedback.reason: Greedy candidates need a local comparison that remains meaningful globally.

blocks.text: An additive or dominance-friendly objective can support an invariant or exchange proof. The shape is only a signal; it is not by itself a proof.

Irreversibility guarantees the local choice is optimal.
Irreversible choices require no state tracking.

Why the key name is easy to understand.
Why the original order is preserved.
Why comparing two keys is constant time.

blocks.text: The explanation must connect the key to future feasibility and value. Runtime and naming do not establish that relationship.
